problem: Social robot navigation is benchmarked with ad-hoc analytic metrics (success, safety, proxemics) that ignore task and context, lack empirical validation against human perception, and are inconsistently chosen by authors. No dataset of human-rated full robot trajectories exists to learn a metric from.
motivation: A standardized, empirically validated benchmark metric is needed so that SocNav policies can be compared fairly and optimized (e.g. via RL/MPC). The authors propose an All-encompassing Learned Trajectory-wise (ALT) metric learned directly from human ratings of whole trajectories, conditioned on context.
key_idea: Collect and release a specification and dataset of human-rated social navigation trajectories with free-text context, and train a GRU on them (SN26) to predict human scores as a learned, context-aware trajectory-level metric.
insight: Learned metric correlates far better with human scores (Pearson 0.797, Spearman 0.684) than any analytic metric (best |r| 0.415). Ablations show collision and social-space-intrusion features (CCC 0.776 to 0.650/0.652) and success features (CCC 0.681) matter most, while LLM-derived context features matter little (e.g. Urgency removal CCC 0.774), probably because of LLM inconsistencies.
method: Dataset specification: JSON format for robot (pose, speed, drive, shape), task (go-to/guide-to/follow/interact-with with goal), humans (2D pose, optional 3D keypoints), objects (text description, pose, shape), walls, grid map, area semantics, plus rater demographics and scores in [0,1].

SocNavData2026: 4427 trajectories (182 real from Aston lab and SACSoN, 4245 simulated from SocNavGym, HATEB, HuNavSim, Gazebo), extended to 7472 by varying walls; go-to tasks only, indoor 6-10 m areas; 4402 scored trajectories after quality filtering.
Rater quality assurance: 49 raters; discards those missing control questions, then filters by quadratic weighted Cohen's kappa intra- and inter-rater thresholds (0.4/0.1/0.2), leaving 22 raters.

Input features: per-step vector x_t = trajectory features (pose, speed, accel in goal frame, thresholds, flags, step ratio) || analytic metric features (distances, collisions, intrusions, TTC, cost of fear/panic, path efficiency) || LLM context embedding.

Context embedding: Claude 3.7 Sonnet is prompted to output a percentile for 10 aspects (urgency, risk, human distance, speed, bumping justification, etc.) from the free-text task context, normalized to 0-1.

SN26 model: 4-layer GRU (256 hidden) with the last-step output fed into an MLP (256 hidden, sigmoid output); MSE loss, lr 1e-5, batch 32, early stopping patience 20, mirror augmentation, 0.9/0.05/0.05 split with no leakage between trajectory variants.
Software tools: visualizer, statistical analysis scripts, surveying tool, normalization and augmentation transforms.

setting.backbone: GRU (4 layers, 256 hidden) + MLP trained from scratch; Claude 3.7 Sonnet (frozen) for context features
setting.training_data: SocNavData2026: 7472 trajectory variants (182 real + 4245 simulated base trajectories) with 4402 human-rated trajectories from 22 raters
setting.observation: Top-down structured trajectory data (robot/human/object poses, walls, task context text); not sensor input
setting.simulator: SocNavGym, HATEB, HuNavSim, Gazebo (data source), plus real recordings
setting.privileged: Uses ground-truth human/object poses and map of the scenario as inputs to the metric

numbers_note: Not a navigation-benchmark paper; results are metric-prediction quality on its own test set (MSE 0.0457, MAE 0.160, Pearson 0.797, Spearman 0.684), which do not map to a canonical benchmark.
results: SN26 achieves test MSE 0.0457 and MAE 0.160, and MSE 0.0053 / MAE 0.053 against the mean of control questions. Its Pearson/Spearman correlation with human scores (0.797/0.684) far exceeds analytic metrics such as max near humans (A) (-0.415) and collisions (about -0.385). Qualitatively it distinguishes contexts (lab, fire, office, fragile) and speed/proxemics trade-offs.
limitations: Small proof-of-concept dataset: only go-to tasks, indoor 6-10 m areas, limited object types, mostly simulated trajectories; 5% test split (~200 trajectories) and random split.
More sophisticated architectures did not work, likely due to data size; context features from LLM are inconsistent and contribute little.
Policy development using the metric is not evaluated; no validation on external held-out datasets.
builds_on: Francis et al. principles for social navigation (ALT metric)
compares_to: analytic SocNav metrics (success, collisions, social space intrusion, min distance, TTC, cost of fear/panic, path efficiency)
version: deepread-v1 (2026-09-29): full text + insight + evidence-checked numbers
